assessment.nobel_worthiness: A highly consequential account of how trade and technology reshape tasks, employment, and wage inequality, with broad influence on research and public understanding.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn, and Hanson are central and complementary contributors to the identified empirical and conceptual agenda; the broader literature makes precise boundaries necessarily imperfect.
assessment.maturity: The findings have accumulated over a substantial period and have been tested across settings and subsequent work.
uncertainties: The relative contributions of trade, automation, institutions, and local adjustment remain difficult to separate fully.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative-data research transformed measurement of intergenerational mobility and made geographic and institutional differences in opportunity central economic facts.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren, and Friedman are strongly identified with the construction and interpretation of this research program, though it rests on wider collaborative data work.
assessment.maturity: The core measurements and empirical regularities have had time to diffuse widely and support extensive follow-on research.
uncertainties: Interpretation of mobility measures and causal pathways from place to opportunity remains contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The long-run reconstruction of income and wealth concentration substantially changed the empirical basis for studying inequality, taxation, and distribution.
assessment.attribution: Piketty, Saez, and Zucman are leading contributors to the linked historical-data, top-income, and offshore-wealth agenda, while important antecedents and collaborators complicate any small allocation.
assessment.maturity: The data-building effort, methods, and scholarly consequences are well established across a long research horizon.
uncertainties: Wealth capitalization, tax-record coverage, and offshore-wealth estimates involve consequential measurement assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gave a powerful quantitative language for connecting firm-level distortions to large cross-country income differences.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh, Klenow, and Restuccia are core architects of the agenda represented here, with recognizable but related contributions.
assessment.maturity: The framework has generated a large subsequent literature and remains a benchmark in development and growth research.
uncertainties: Measured wedges may reflect technology, adjustment costs, or data limitations rather than policy-relevant distortions alone.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Research on management practices made organizational capital empirically measurable and connected it convincingly to productivity and development.
assessment.attribution: Bloom, Van Reenen, and Sadun have supplied central evidence and methods for the management-practices program.
assessment.maturity: The agenda has been replicated across countries and developed through experiments, surveys, and firm-level studies.
uncertainties: The extent to which measured management is causal rather than jointly determined with firm quality remains an active question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their work provided durable economic foundations for thinking about exhaustible resources, biodiversity, and wealth inclusive of natural capital.
assessment.attribution: Dasgupta and Heal are clear foundational figures for the contribution as framed.
assessment.maturity: The intellectual contribution is longstanding and increasingly relevant to policy and accounting practice.
uncertainties: Valuing biodiversity and substitutability between natural and produced capital remains empirically and ethically difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The systematic long-run assembly of evidence on financial crises, sovereign debt, and default deeply influenced macroeconomic history and crisis analysis.
assessment.attribution: Reinhart and Rogoff are the unmistakable joint figures associated with this particular comparative historical-crisis enterprise.
assessment.maturity: The research has had substantial scholarly and policy impact over many years.
uncertainties: Some headline empirical claims and data-processing choices have received important criticism, limiting confidence in particular policy inferences.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theoretical and empirical work on monopsony changed the understanding of wage setting, employer power, and the incidence of labour-market policy.
assessment.attribution: Manning is especially central to modern monopsony analysis, while Ashenfelter and Naidu represent influential empirical and institutional extensions.
assessment.maturity: The agenda is well established and has become central to current labour-economics research and policy debates.
uncertainties: The prevalence and magnitude of employer power vary sharply across labour markets and empirical designs.
